outputs.L1:
WASHINGTON (CNN) — Pakistan is optimistic about the Obama administration’s commitment to the region and is prepared to work with the United States to help root out extremism within its borders, Pakistan’s foreign minister said.

Pakistani Foreign Minister Makhdoom Shah Mehmood Qureshi met with U.S. Secretary of State Hillary Clinton. Following the meeting, Qureshi cited a “convergence of interests” between Washington and Islamabad, as well as a shared “willingness to work together.”

“I see a lot of hope in the new administration, the new leadership, and Pakistan is willing to work with the American administration to fight extremism and terrorism,” he said Tuesday. “We are determined to defeat terrorism in all its forms and manifestations.”

Qureshi is in Washington to participate in a strategic review of U.S. policy aimed at stabilizing Afghanistan and neighboring Pakistan. The effort is being led by South Asian security expert Bruce Reidel and Ambassador Richard Holbrooke, the U.S. special envoy.

Afghan Foreign Minister Rangin D. Spanta is also leading a delegation from his country to take part in the review. He and Qureshi are scheduled to meet with both Clinton and Holbrooke this week.

U.S. President Barack Obama and Clinton appointed Holbrooke as special representative for the two countries, underscoring the new administration’s view that Afghanistan and Pakistan are closely intertwined in any solution to the war in Afghanistan and to the terrorist threat along their shared border.

“We are consulting very closely with the government of Pakistan on our strategic review of our way forward, and I’m very grateful for the minister’s advice and counsel,” Clinton said after meeting with Qureshi.

Last week, Obama announced that he is sending an additional 17,000 troops to Afghanistan to combat a strengthening insurgency, which he has described as the “central front in our enduring struggle against terrorism and extremism.” The troops will be deployed to southern Afghanistan, which borders Pakistan and serves as a haven for Taliban insurgents.

Pakistani officials have expressed concern that the deployment could push the Taliban across the border into Pakistan and further destabilize their country.

The Obama administration is conducting several reviews of U.S. policy in Afghanistan, including one led by Gen. David Petraeus, the commander in the region. Defense Secretary Robert Gates has said the original mission in Afghanistan was “too broad” and needs to be more “realistic and focused” for the United States to succeed.

Pakistan is engaged in its own campaign against Taliban militants in its Northwest Frontier Province. The militants, who effectively control the country’s Swat Valley, extended a cease-fire Tuesday as part of an agreement with the government — a deal that the United States and NATO have warned risks granting extremists a safe haven near the Afghan border.

Swat Valley was once one of Pakistan’s leading tourist destinations. It is located near the Afghanistan border and about 186 miles, or 300 kilometers, from Pakistan’s capital, Islamabad.

In recent months, militants have unleashed a wave of violence across the province, claiming hundreds of lives. They seek to require veils for women and beards for men, and to ban music and television. The fighting has displaced nearly half of Swat’s population, officials said.

The central government has long exercised limited control in the area, but in late July it launched an intense military offensive to drive out militants. In retaliation for the military presence, the Taliban carried out a series of deadly bombings, beheadings and kidnappings, and said the attacks would continue until the troops withdrew.

On Tuesday, the Taliban said it was indefinitely extending a cease-fire that its leaders had declared eight days earlier, after signing a controversial agreement with the government to impose Islamic law, or Sharia, in the region.

The Pakistani government’s decision to negotiate has drawn international criticism. Holbrooke has said the Obama administration was “troubled and confused” by the truce in Swat. Holbrooke and NATO officials have also expressed concern that such an accord could effectively cede control of the Swat Valley to extremists.

“We are consulting very closely with the government of Pakistan on our strategic review of our way forward and I'm very grateful for the minister's advice and counsel,” Clinton said after her meeting with Qureshi.

The previous week, Obama announced that an additional 17,000 U.S. troops would be deployed to Afghanistan to confront a growing insurgency. Obama has described Afghanistan as the “central front in our enduring struggle against terrorism and extremism.”

Those forces are to be sent to southern Afghanistan, an area bordering Pakistan that has served as a refuge for Taliban insurgents. Pakistani officials have voiced worries that the new deployment could drive Taliban fighters over the border into Pakistan, worsening instability there.

The Obama administration is carrying out multiple reviews of U.S. strategy in Afghanistan, including one led by Gen. David Petraeus, the regional commander. Defense Secretary Robert Gates has said the initial U.S. mission in Afghanistan was “too broad” and must become more “realistic and focused” if the United States is to succeed.

Pakistan, meanwhile, is conducting its own campaign against Taliban militants in its Northwest Frontier Province. The militants, who effectively dominate the country’s Swat Valley, extended a cease-fire Tuesday under an agreement with the government. U.S. and NATO officials have warned that the arrangement could give extremists a secure base near the Afghan border.

Swat Valley was formerly one of Pakistan’s major tourist areas. It lies near the Afghan border and about 186 miles, or 300 kilometers, from Islamabad, Pakistan’s capital.

In recent months, militants have carried out extensive violence across the province, killing hundreds of people. They seek to force women to wear veils, require men to grow beards, and prohibit music and television.

Officials said the conflict has forced almost half of Swat’s residents from their homes. The central government has historically had limited authority in the area, but in late July it began a major military operation intended to drive militants out.

In response to the military presence, the Taliban launched deadly bombings, beheadings and kidnappings, and said such attacks would go on until troops withdrew.

On Tuesday, the Taliban said it would extend a cease-fire indefinitely. Taliban leaders had first announced the truce eight days earlier, after reaching a disputed agreement with the government to introduce Islamic law, or Sharia, in the region.

The Pakistani government’s decision to negotiate has drawn criticism from abroad. Holbrooke has said the Obama administration was “troubled and confused” by the Swat truce. Both Holbrooke and NATO officials have warned that the agreement could effectively hand control of Swat Valley to extremists.

**Pakistan’s foreign minister meets Clinton in Washington amid concerns over extremism**

**Washington** — Pakistan’s foreign minister met with U.S. Secretary of State Hillary Clinton in Washington on Tuesday for talks focused on countering extremism, stabilizing Afghanistan and assessing a controversial cease-fire with Taliban militants in Pakistan’s Swat Valley.

The visit comes as the Obama administration seeks to strengthen cooperation with Pakistan, a key but often complicated partner in U.S. efforts to combat al Qaeda and Taliban-linked groups operating along the Pakistan-Afghanistan border.

Foreign Minister Shah Mahmood Qureshi said Pakistan remained committed to fighting terrorism and extremism, but stressed that military measures alone would not resolve the crisis. He called for broader economic assistance, political support and development initiatives aimed at addressing the conditions that allow militant groups to gain influence.

Clinton said the United States viewed Pakistan’s stability as central to regional security and pledged continued engagement with Islamabad. U.S. officials have repeatedly said that Pakistan’s cooperation is essential to the administration’s strategy in Afghanistan, where American forces are battling a resilient Taliban insurgency.

A major topic of discussion was the Pakistani government’s cease-fire arrangement in the Swat Valley, a once-popular tourist region in northwestern Pakistan where Taliban militants have expanded their control. The agreement, which included the implementation of Islamic law in parts of the region, has drawn concern from U.S. officials and human rights groups who worry it could embolden militants rather than contain them.

Pakistani officials have defended the deal as an attempt to restore calm and create space for local governance after months of violence. But Washington has pressed Islamabad to ensure that any agreement does not provide safe haven to extremist groups or undermine the rights of residents, particularly women and girls.

The talks also touched on Afghanistan, where the Obama administration has ordered a renewed focus on defeating extremist networks and strengthening Afghan institutions. U.S. officials have emphasized that the conflict cannot be addressed solely within Afghanistan’s borders, pointing to militant sanctuaries in Pakistan’s tribal areas and northwest as a persistent threat.

Qureshi’s visit is part of a broader diplomatic push as the new U.S. administration reassesses its policy toward South Asia. Obama officials have signaled they want a more comprehensive approach that links security assistance with economic development, democratic governance and regional diplomacy.

Both sides described the meeting as constructive, though significant challenges remain. Pakistan faces rising militant violence, domestic political pressure and public skepticism toward U.S. policy, including anger over American drone strikes. The United States, meanwhile, has urged Pakistan to take sustained action against militant groups while offering increased assistance to help strengthen the country’s civilian government.

The discussions underscored the high stakes for both governments: preventing extremist groups from expanding their influence, stabilizing Afghanistan and ensuring that Pakistan remains a reliable partner in a volatile region.

## U.S.-Pakistan talks focus on Afghanistan strategy as Swat deal raises alarms

**Washington** — Senior U.S. and Pakistani officials held high-level talks during the early months of the Obama administration as Washington sought to reshape its strategy for Afghanistan and Pakistan, placing both countries at the center of a widening regional security challenge.

At the heart of the discussions was Richard Holbrooke, President Barack Obama’s special representative for Afghanistan and Pakistan, who was tasked with coordinating U.S. diplomatic efforts in a region increasingly viewed by the White House as a single, interconnected theater of conflict.

Holbrooke’s role reflected a shift in U.S. thinking: the war in Afghanistan could not be stabilized without addressing militant sanctuaries, political instability and military operations across the border in Pakistan.

### Obama expands Afghan war effort

The talks came as Obama approved a significant increase in U.S. forces in Afghanistan, ordering thousands of additional troops to counter a resurgent Taliban insurgency. The administration argued that security conditions had deteriorated and that the United States needed a stronger military presence, along with expanded training for Afghan security forces.

U.S. officials described the troop increase as part of a broader strategy that combined military pressure, civilian aid, regional diplomacy and governance reforms. But the move also raised questions about whether more forces would be enough to reverse years of Taliban gains, particularly if militants continued to find refuge in Pakistan’s tribal areas and border regions.

Pakistan, meanwhile, remained wary of U.S. pressure. Pakistani leaders insisted they were fighting extremism on their own soil, but they also faced strong domestic opposition to policies seen as aligned too closely with Washington.

### Holbrooke pushes regional approach

Holbrooke, a veteran diplomat best known for his role in the Balkans during the Clinton administration, pushed for a comprehensive approach to what U.S. officials increasingly called the “AfPak” problem.

His mandate included encouraging cooperation between Afghanistan and Pakistan, coordinating with NATO allies, and pressing Islamabad to take stronger action against extremist groups operating from Pakistani territory.

But Holbrooke faced a complicated political landscape. Pakistan’s civilian government was fragile, its military retained dominant influence over national security policy, and public anger toward U.S. drone strikes and American involvement was growing.

U.S. officials also had to balance security demands with the need to support Pakistan’s democracy and economy. Washington viewed Pakistan as a critical partner, but trust between the two countries remained limited.

### Swat Valley deal draws U.S. concern

Adding urgency to the talks was Pakistan’s controversial agreement to allow the implementation of Islamic law in the Swat Valley, a once-popular tourist region that had fallen under the influence of Taliban-linked militants.

The deal, reached between Pakistani authorities and local Islamist representatives, was intended to end violence in the region by permitting a form of Sharia-based justice under the Nizam-e-Adl regulation. Supporters in Pakistan argued that the agreement could bring peace to an area where the state had struggled to maintain control.

But critics warned that the deal amounted to a dangerous concession to militants. Human rights groups expressed concern that it could undermine women’s rights, weaken Pakistan’s legal system and embolden extremists elsewhere in the country.

U.S. officials reacted cautiously but with clear unease. The Obama administration was concerned that allowing militants to dictate terms in Swat could signal weakness and create a model for similar arrangements in other contested areas.

### Pakistan caught between pressure and politics

For Pakistan’s government, the Swat deal underscored the difficult balance between military action and political compromise. Pakistani forces had launched operations against militants in the region, but the violence displaced civilians and strained public support.

Islamabad argued that local solutions were necessary in some areas, especially where courts were slow and governance was weak. But Washington feared that any agreement granting space to militants could threaten broader regional security.

The issue became a test of Pakistan’s willingness and ability to confront extremist groups not only in remote tribal areas, but also in settled regions closer to the country’s political heartland.

### A fragile partnership

The U.S.-Pakistan relationship during the Obama administration’s early months was defined by mutual dependence and deep suspicion. The United States needed Pakistan’s cooperation to support the war in Afghanistan, disrupt al Qaeda and pressure Taliban networks. Pakistan needed U.S. military and economic assistance but resisted being seen as acting under American orders.

Holbrooke’s diplomatic mission was to manage that tension while building support for a strategy that linked battlefield gains in Afghanistan with political stability in Pakistan.

Whether that approach could succeed remained uncertain. The troop increase signaled Obama’s commitment to Afghanistan, but the Swat deal highlighted the growing complexity of Pakistan’s internal battle against militancy.

For Washington, the message was increasingly clear: the future of the Afghan war would be shaped not only in Kabul and Kandahar, but also in Islamabad, Peshawar and the valleys of northwestern Pakistan.

**Pakistan Welcomes Obama’s Regional Strategy as Swat Truce Draws Sharp Criticism**

*Islamabad* — Pakistan signaled cautious optimism Tuesday over President Barack Obama’s emerging strategy for Afghanistan and Pakistan, even as Islamabad faced mounting criticism at home and abroad over a controversial cease-fire agreement with Taliban militants in the Swat Valley.

Pakistani officials said they were encouraged by the Obama administration’s stated intention to approach the conflict in Afghanistan and Pakistan as a single regional challenge, rather than treating the two countries in isolation. The shift, they said, could open the door to greater cooperation on security, economic development and counterterrorism.

“We have consistently argued that peace and stability in Afghanistan are inseparable from peace and stability in Pakistan,” a senior Pakistani official said. “If the new U.S. administration is prepared to recognize the regional nature of the problem, that is a welcome development.”

The comments came as Washington reviewed policy options for a war that has steadily spilled across the Afghan border into Pakistan’s tribal areas and northwestern districts. Obama, who has pledged to refocus U.S. attention on Afghanistan, is expected to increase American troop levels there while also pressing Pakistan to do more against al-Qaida and Taliban sanctuaries on its soil.

Pakistani leaders have publicly welcomed the prospect of a broader strategy that includes development aid and political engagement, not just military pressure. But they have also warned against expanded U.S. drone strikes or unilateral American action inside Pakistan, arguing that such measures inflame public anger and undermine Islamabad’s ability to confront militancy.

That balancing act has become especially delicate after authorities in Pakistan’s North West Frontier Province reached a cease-fire with Taliban-linked militants in Swat, a once-popular tourist region that has fallen increasingly under insurgent control.

Under the deal, provincial authorities agreed to support the implementation of Islamic law, or sharia, in the Malakand region, which includes Swat, in exchange for an end to militant attacks. The arrangement was negotiated with Sufi Muhammad, a pro-Taliban cleric whose movement has long demanded Islamic courts in the area. His son-in-law, Maulana Fazlullah, leads the Taliban faction blamed for a brutal campaign of beheadings, school bombings and attacks on security forces.

Supporters of the agreement say it could bring badly needed relief to civilians after months of fighting that displaced thousands and left much of Swat under de facto militant rule. They argue that the demand for swift Islamic justice has roots in local frustration with Pakistan’s slow and often corrupt court system, and that a negotiated pause could create space for restoring government authority.

But critics accuse the government of capitulating to extremists.

Human rights groups, opposition figures and some Western officials warned that the accord could embolden militants and allow them to consolidate control over Swat. They expressed particular concern about the fate of women and girls in the valley, where militants have destroyed or closed scores of girls’ schools and enforced harsh social restrictions.

“The danger is that this is being presented as a peace deal when it may in fact be a surrender of citizens’ rights,” said one Pakistani rights activist. “The people of Swat need security and justice, but not at the cost of handing power to armed groups.”

The United States has reacted warily. American officials have repeatedly said that past agreements with militants in Pakistan’s tribal belt gave insurgents time to regroup and launch attacks on both Pakistani and NATO forces across the border in Afghanistan.

Pakistan’s government insists the Swat accord is not a concession to militancy but an attempt to address local grievances while separating reconcilable elements from hard-core extremists. Officials say any agreement must require militants to lay down arms and accept the writ of the state.

Still, the timing has complicated Islamabad’s message to Washington. As Pakistan seeks to demonstrate that it is a reliable partner in a new regional strategy, the Swat cease-fire has raised questions about whether the government has the will — or the capacity — to confront Taliban influence beyond the tribal areas.

The debate reflects Pakistan’s broader dilemma: military operations have often caused civilian casualties and displacement, deepening resentment toward the state, while peace deals have repeatedly been criticized for allowing militants to expand their reach.

For Obama, the issue underscores the difficulty of crafting a regional approach that depends heavily on Pakistani cooperation while recognizing Pakistan’s domestic political constraints. Anti-American sentiment remains high in much of the country, fueled by drone strikes, civilian casualties and the perception that Pakistan is being asked to fight a U.S.-led war.

Pakistani officials argue that any durable strategy must include more economic assistance, support for democratic institutions and a greater effort to resolve regional disputes, including tensions with India. They say militancy cannot be defeated by force alone.

Analysts say Islamabad’s optimism about Obama’s policy reflects hope that Washington will move away from what many Pakistanis viewed as the Bush administration’s overly narrow focus on military operations and counterterrorism.

“The Pakistani government wants to hear that the United States is thinking politically and economically, not just militarily,” said a regional security analyst in Islamabad. “But the Swat deal sends a mixed signal. It may calm the area temporarily, or it may convince militants that pressure works.”

For residents of Swat, the immediate concern is whether the cease-fire will hold. Many families have fled the fighting, schools have been shut, and local officials have struggled to maintain basic services. Some residents cautiously welcomed the lull in violence, saying any pause was preferable to constant clashes. Others feared that the agreement would leave them at the mercy of militants who have already imposed their authority through fear.

As Islamabad looks toward a new phase in relations with Washington, the contrast is stark: Pakistan is embracing the language of regional cooperation and long-term stability, while confronting accusations that, in Swat, it has chosen short-term calm over the harder task of defeating militancy.

Whether the cease-fire becomes a stepping stone toward peace or another setback in Pakistan’s battle against the Taliban may shape not only the future of Swat, but also the credibility of Obama’s regional strategy.

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a wire-service style report summarizing Hillary Clinton’s meeting with Pakistan’s foreign minister, the U.S. strategic review on Afghanistan and Pakistan, and the security situation in Pakistan’s Northwest Frontier Province.
counterfactuals.output:
WASHINGTON — U.S. Secretary of State Hillary Clinton met Pakistan’s foreign minister for talks focused on the Obama administration’s review of policy toward Afghanistan and Pakistan, as Washington weighed how to counter a worsening militant threat along the two countries’ border.

Clinton’s meeting with Foreign Minister Shah Mahmood Qureshi came as the United States conducted a broad strategic review of its approach to the region, including military operations in Afghanistan, cross-border militant sanctuaries in Pakistan’s tribal areas and expanded civilian assistance to Islamabad.

U.S. officials have said the review is intended to produce a more integrated strategy for Afghanistan and Pakistan, treating the insurgency on both sides of the border as a linked challenge. The administration has emphasized the need for closer cooperation with Pakistan while also pressing Islamabad to act against Taliban and al Qaeda-linked groups operating from its territory.

Pakistan has sought greater U.S. economic and military support, arguing that instability is driven not only by militancy but also by poverty, weak governance and the spillover from years of conflict in Afghanistan. Pakistani officials have also objected to U.S. missile strikes in border areas, saying they inflame public anger even when they target militant leaders.

The talks took place against a deteriorating security backdrop in Pakistan’s Northwest Frontier Province, where Taliban-linked militants have expanded their influence beyond the tribal belt. The Swat Valley, once a tourist destination, has seen heavy fighting, assassinations of local officials, attacks on schools and the displacement of civilians.

A provincial deal aimed at ending violence in Swat by allowing the implementation of Islamic law has drawn concern in Washington and among Pakistani critics, who fear it could embolden militants and weaken state authority. Pakistani officials have defended such arrangements as tactical efforts to restore calm, while insisting they remain committed to combating terrorism.

The United States views Pakistan as central to its Afghanistan strategy because insurgent networks use remote Pakistani border regions for training, planning and resupply. Washington is expected to pair additional troops in Afghanistan with increased diplomatic engagement and development aid for Pakistan, while seeking stronger action against militant safe havens.

Clinton’s discussions with Qureshi were part of a wider diplomatic push as the administration prepared to define its regional policy. U.S. officials have said any durable solution will require improved security, better governance and economic development on both sides of the border.
